title: Linear Equations in Two Variables, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with equations in two variables, and then a fast way to find intercepts and test points with Desmos.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it's so tempting.

scenes.title: Trap 1: the sign of the slope

beats.say: Trap one. In standard form, the slope is negative A over B. For two x plus five y equals twenty, students often forget the minus sign.
The slope is negative two over five. You can confirm by solving for y. Five y equals negative two x plus twenty, so y equals negative two fifths x plus four.
Trap two. The perpendicular slope to two fifths isn't five halves. That only flips the fraction, and the sign stays the same.
A negative reciprocal needs both steps. Flip the fraction and change the sign, so the perpendicular slope is negative five halves. The two slopes multiply to negative one.
Trap three. In four x minus three y equals twenty-four, setting x to zero gives negative three y equals twenty-four. Students sometimes report the x-intercept as the y-intercept.
The y-intercept comes from x equals zero, so y equals twenty-four divided by negative three, which is negative eight. The value six comes from setting y to zero.
Trap four. The line three x plus k y equals twenty-one passes through the point three comma two. Students sometimes swap the coordinates when they substitute.
In the point three comma two, x is three and y is two. So we substitute three for x and two for y, which gives nine plus two k equals twenty-one, and k equals six.
Trap five. In eight a plus five c equals two hundred, suppose c is on the horizontal axis. The horizontal intercept is the value of c when a is zero, but students read the wrong one.
Set a to zero. Five c equals two hundred, so c equals forty. The horizontal intercept is the point where c equals forty.
beats.right_why: Axis variable when the other is 0

beats.say: Desmos graphs standard form directly, with no rearranging. You can click the grey dots on the axes to read the intercepts, and you can plot a point to see whether it sits on the line.
Our first example is the line six x minus three y equals twelve. We want both of its intercepts.
Open a fresh graph. We'll type the equation exactly as it's written in standard form.
Type six x minus three y equals twelve. Desmos draws the line, and there's no need to rearrange the equation.
Click the line, then click the grey dot where it meets the x axis. Desmos shows the point two comma zero, so the x-intercept is two.
Now click the grey dot on the y axis. Desmos shows zero comma negative four, so the y-intercept is negative four.
Both intercepts match our algebra from part one, and we found them without solving anything.
Desmos is also handy for story equations. For eight a plus five c equals two hundred, if fifteen adult tickets were sold, we can graph the equation and the line x equals fifteen.
We use x for adult tickets and y for child tickets. First type the equation for the total sales.
Now type x equals fifteen. That's a vertical line, showing the case of fifteen adult tickets.
Click where the two lines cross, and then click the grey dot. Desmos shows fifteen comma sixteen, so sixteen child tickets were sold.
That matches our answer from the previous video. The graph gave us the same result in two typed lines.
Now a practice problem. Find the slope and both intercepts of two x plus five y equals twenty. Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
Set x to zero to find where the line crosses the y axis.
Two times zero is zero, so the x term disappears and we're left with five y equals twenty.
Divide both sides by five. Twenty divided by five is four. So the y-intercept is four.
Set y to zero to find where the line crosses the x axis.
Five times zero is zero, so the y term disappears and we're left with two x equals twenty.
Divide both sides by two. Twenty divided by two is ten. So the x-intercept is ten. The slope is negative two over five, from negative A over B.
To recap. The slope in standard form is negative A over B, and perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals.
Set x to zero for the y-intercept, and set y to zero for the x-intercept. Substitute x and y carefully, in the right places.
beats.item: Intercepts: zero out the other variable

beats.say: Desmos reads intercepts and story equations quickly. In the next topic, we study systems of two linear equations.
